name: UPF clothing

card.summary: Fabric tested and labelled for how much UV it blocks, used as a no-reapplication alternative to sunscreen.
card.aka: Sun-protective clothing, UV-protective clothing, sun shirts, rash guards
card.note: Protection depends on weave, colour, fit and wetness; wet or stretched fabric blocks less.

quick.overview:
UPF clothing is made from fabric tested for ultraviolet protection factor, a lab measure of how much sunburn-causing UV passes through the cloth. UPF 50+ is the top published category, rated as blocking at least about 98 percent of UV.

People who want to limit sun-related skin ageing, uneven pigmentation or skin cancer risk without applying sunscreen to covered areas use it, along with hats and shade. Evidence that clothing reduces UV reaching skin is strong in laboratory terms; direct trials of appearance outcomes are limited.
quick.mechanism: Fabric absorbs, reflects or scatters UV. Denser weave, darker colour, heavier weight and added UV absorbers raise the rating, while stretching, wetting and wear can lower it. Ratings are measured with instruments rather than by testing sunburn on people.
quick.risks: The clothing itself carries little risk. Documented limits are reduced protection when wet or stretched, heat retention in heavy dark fabrics, and uncovered skin remaining exposed. Standards in North America are industry-led test methods rather than a government approval.

lead: UPF clothing, also called sun-protective clothing, is apparel made from fabrics rated for ultraviolet protection. The ultraviolet protection factor (UPF) is the ratio of sunburn-causing UV that passes through a fabric without it versus with it, similar in concept to sunscreen's SPF but measured with laboratory instruments rather than human sunburn testing.[1]

Under the American ASTM classification, UPF 15 to 24 is rated good, 25 to 39 very good, and 40 to 50+ excellent, blocking roughly 93 to 98 percent or more of UV.[1] Fabric factors that influence the rating include fibre content, weave, colour, finishing and additives, and the performance of a fabric changes with stretching, shrinkage, hydration, laundering and wear.[1][2] A review from 1998 noted that an average-weight cotton T-shirt gives an SPF of about 7.[2]

Sun-protective clothing is promoted for preventing sunburn, photoaging and skin cancer, and dermatology reviews list sun-protective clothing among recommended photoprotection measures including for skin of color.[3] Randomized trials have tested clothing in children and behaviour programmes, but no trial reviewed measured appearance outcomes such as wrinkles or pigmentation.

paras: Sun-protective garments include long-sleeved shirts, rash guards, swimwear, hats, pants and gloves. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes both everyday items and specialised variants for beach and outdoor-labour use.[5]

UV protection is built into the fabric through tight weaves and, in some products, UV-absorbing finishes or additives. In 2003 BASF introduced a nylon with titanium dioxide nanoparticles that stayed protective when wet.[1]

Wikipedia reports that sun-protective clothing became popular in Australia as a complement to sunscreen, with a laboratory testing procedure set by ARPANSA in 1996.[1] The UK set a standard in 1998 through the National Radiological Protection Board and the British Standards Institute, and the US formal standard followed in 2001, adding tests for durability, abrasion and washing.[1]
Before UPF testing, clothing was rated by SPF-style measures of how long skin took to redden.[1]

UPF measures UV transmission through fabric. Denser weave and darker colour usually protect more, and wetting can reduce protection by as much as half for most fabrics, with silk and viscose noted as exceptions.[1] Visible-light appearance does not reliably indicate UV blocking.[1]
Skin Cancer Foundation recommendations, as summarised by Grokipedia, call for UPF 50+ garments for its Seal of Recommendation, and garments are tested for at least 40 launderings.[5]

Laboratory UPF testing shows that fabric type affects how much UV reaches the skin.[2] Dermatology reviews describe sun-protective clothing, hats and shade as components of photoprotection recommended alongside sunscreen, including for people with darker skin, who can be affected by hyperpigmentation disorders.[3]
A review of cutaneous melanoma notes UV exposure and indoor tanning as risk factors and lists avoidance of direct sun, sunscreen and sun-protective clothing among primary prevention measures.[6]

The North Queensland Sun-Safe Clothing study is a randomized trial in Townsville, Australia, that gave 652 young children garments made from fabrics rated very good to excellent for UV protection in 13 child-care centres, compared with 12 usual-care centres, with new moles as the main outcome; its baseline report found the groups similar at the start.[7] No outcome result from that trial is included in the report reviewed here.

Other randomized trials have tested education and school or family programmes that promote protective clothing and sunscreen, and a survey study found that women were more willing to consider handheld umbrellas after seeing photographs of famous women carrying them.[8][9][10] A Cochrane review has examined sun protection measures for preventing basal and squamous cell skin cancers.[4] No published trials were found comparing UPF clothing with other measures on wrinkles or skin tone.

Limitations reported include reduced protection when fabric is wet or stretched, heat retention in heavy dark garments, and the fact that clothing protects only covered skin.[1] Wikipedia notes that the North American industry is self-regulated under AATCC and ASTM methods.[1]

No community discussion of UPF clothing was found in the sources reviewed. Photoprotection is generally discussed in appearance communities under sunscreen and skincare, and UPF clothing is described by Grokipedia as helping to preserve collagen and skin appearance by limiting UV exposure.[5]
